opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The key insight is that physical phenomena are fundamentally continuous. When you write down a partial differential equation for fluid flow, weather, or material deformation, you're describing functions in space and time, not pixels on a fixed grid. Standard neural networks, though, learn mappings between finite-dimensional vectors, so they get tied to whatever resolution you trained them on.

Neural operators instead learn mappings between function spaces. You learn the operator itself, the map from an initial condition or a set of coefficients to the solution, and that gives you discretization invariance. You can train on data at one resolution and query the model at a different one, even a finer one, and it still behaves sensibly. That property is what makes it natural to work across scales.

Take the Fourier Neural Operator. We do the learned transformations in the frequency domain, where you can capture global, long-range interactions efficiently. That matters because in turbulence, say, energy cascades across scales. Small eddies influence large structures and vice versa, and a purely local convolution has a hard time with that. Working in the spectral domain gives you that multiscale coupling naturally.

There's also a practical reason. In science we never have clean, uniform data. You might have coarse simulation data that's cheap to generate, a handful of expensive high-fidelity runs, and some experimental measurements on irregular meshes. A neural operator lets you combine all of these, because it's not locked to a single discretization. And you can add physics-informed losses on top, so even where data is sparse, the model is constrained by the governing equations, which helps it extrapolate to finer scales than you had data for.

The payoff is speed. We've seen speedups of several orders of magnitude, in weather forecasting with FourCastNet and in applications like carbon capture and storage, while keeping accuracy competitive with traditional numerical solvers. That opens up things that were simply impossible before: large ensembles for uncertainty quantification, real-time design optimization, inverse problems. So to me neural operators aren't just a faster solver. They're the right mathematical framework for bringing AI into science, because they respect the continuous, multiscale nature of the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response says a neural operator can be trained at one resolution and queried at another, and can combine data from different discretizations in the same model.

r002.rationale: It discusses coarse and fine resolutions and multiscale phenomena, but does not explain that simulation resolution determines which physical phenomena can be captured.

r003.rationale: It says standard networks are tied to a trained resolution, but does not identify a fixed pixel representation as limiting finer detail when zooming in.

r004.rationale: It explains that neural operators map between function spaces and can be queried at a finer resolution than the one used for training.

r005.rationale: It mentions physics-informed losses and extrapolation to finer scales, but does not say higher-resolution physical constraints supply finer-scale detail.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that the physical world isn't defined on a grid. When we write down the laws of physics, we write them as differential equations over continuous functions, and the grid is something we impose afterward because computers need discrete numbers. Traditional neural networks inherit that limitation. You train a convolutional network at one resolution, and it's stuck there, because the weights are tied to a specific discretization of the domain.

A neural operator is a different object. Instead of learning a map between finite-dimensional vectors, it learns a map between function spaces. The input is a function, like an initial condition or a coefficient field, and the output is a function, like the solution at a later time. The architecture is built so that it is consistent across discretizations. In the Fourier neural operator, for example, we do the key operation in Fourier space, where the modes you keep don't depend on how finely you sampled the data. So you can train on coarse simulations and evaluate on finer ones, or evaluate at points you never saw during training. That's called zero-shot super-resolution, and it falls out of the formulation rather than being bolted on.

That property matters enormously for multiscale problems. Think about turbulence, or weather, or subsurface flow for carbon storage. The interesting physics spans many orders of magnitude in space and time, and it's extremely expensive to resolve all of it with a numerical solver. With neural operators we've been able to learn from mixed-resolution data, capture the large-scale structure, and still generalize to finer detail, because the model has learned something closer to the underlying operator rather than a lookup table at one resolution.

The other piece is speed. Once trained, these models are typically thousands of times faster than the numerical solvers that produced the data. That turns previously impossible things, like running huge ensembles for uncertainty quantification or doing inverse design in a loop, into things you can actually do. And I think that's where the real impact is. Not just replacing a simulation, but changing the kinds of questions we can afford to ask of it.

r001.rationale: It says neural operators can train on coarse simulations, use mixed-resolution data, and evaluate at finer resolutions within the same formulation.

r002.rationale: It contrasts large-scale structure with finer detail, but does not explain that a simulation’s resolution determines which physical phenomena it can capture.

r003.rationale: It says standard networks are tied to a specific discretization and are stuck at the resolution where they were trained, limiting evaluation at finer resolution.

r004.rationale: It explains that neural operators map between function spaces, remain consistent across discretizations, and allow zero-shot super-resolution.

r005.rationale: It does not say that higher-resolution physical constraints supply finer-scale detail.

astra-6.text:
The key idea is that in physics, we’re often learning a mapping between functions. You give me an initial condition or a field describing the material properties, and I want to predict how the system evolves. A neural operator learns that mapping, rather than a mapping between two fixed-size vectors.

That makes it particularly useful across resolutions. You can train on data at one resolution and evaluate the same learned operator on a different mesh. You’re trying to capture the underlying physics rather than tying the model to a particular discretization.

And physical systems have interactions at many scales. Think of a fluid, where large-scale motion interacts with small vortices. With Fourier neural operators, for example, we can represent global interactions through Fourier modes and learn how those features combine.

There is a caveat: evaluating at a finer resolution doesn’t automatically recover physics that was missing from the training data. But this framework gives us a powerful way to share what we learn across resolutions and accelerate simulations, so we can explore many more conditions or designs.

r001.rationale: It says the same learned operator can be evaluated on a different mesh, communicating use across resolutions in a shared model.

r002.rationale: It notes that finer evaluation cannot recover physics missing from training data, but does not explain how simulation resolution determines which phenomena are captured.

r003.rationale: It does not identify fixed pixels in standard neural networks as limiting detail when zooming in.

r004.rationale: It contrasts mapping functions with mapping fixed-size vectors and says the operator can be evaluated on a different mesh, communicating refinement across resolutions.

r005.rationale: It does not say higher-resolution physical constraints provide finer-scale detail; it instead cautions that finer evaluation does not restore missing physics.

sol-6.1.text:
The key idea is that in physical simulation, we’re often learning a mapping between functions. You might start with an initial temperature field and want to predict how that field evolves, or take a material’s properties and predict its deformation. A neural operator learns that mapping, rather than a mapping between two fixed-size vectors.

That gives us a natural way to work across resolutions. We can train on one discretization and evaluate the same learned operator on a finer grid, because the underlying object we’re trying to learn is independent of the grid. Of course, that doesn’t mean we automatically recover every fine-scale feature we’ve never seen—resolving the relevant physics still matters.

And physical systems have both local interactions and long-range effects. Neural operators can capture those interactions efficiently, including through representations in Fourier space. Once trained, they can make predictions much faster than repeatedly running a numerical solver. That’s particularly useful when you need many simulations for design, optimization, or uncertainty quantification.

r001.rationale: It says the same learned operator can be trained on one discretization and evaluated on a finer grid.

r002.rationale: It says resolving relevant physics matters, but does not explain that simulation resolution determines which physical phenomena can be captured.

r003.rationale: It does not identify fixed pixel representations or explain how they limit a standard neural network’s finer detail when zooming in.

r004.rationale: It explains that the operator learns a mapping between functions independent of the grid, allowing evaluation on a finer grid.

r005.rationale: It does not state that higher-resolution physical constraints can supply finer-scale detail.
